headline: Ghana's Thomas Partey denied Canada visa for World Cup game
summary: FIFA confirms the midfielder will miss the match against Panama due to visa issues, with the Canadian government yet to comment.
details: Ghana midfielder Thomas Partey will not play in the World Cup game against Panama on Wednesday after his visa application to enter Canada was refused, FIFA announced on Friday. The player is currently with the Ghana squad in Boston, USA.

FIFA stated that they are not involved in the immigration processes of host countries, including visa adjudications. The Canadian government has not yet responded to requests for comment on the matter.
Partey will be eligible to play in Ghana's subsequent Group L matches against England in Boston and Croatia in Philadelphia. The 32-year-old former Arsenal player currently plays for Villarreal.
The midfielder faces allegations of rape and sexual assault in the United Kingdom, which he has denied. This legal situation may be a factor in the visa refusal.
caption:
Ghana's Thomas Partey ruled out of World Cup clash after visa refusal.

FIFA confirms the midfielder cannot travel to Canada for the match against Panama.

Ghana midfielder Thomas Partey will not play in the World Cup game against Panama on Wednesday after his visa application to enter Canada was refused, FIFA announced on Friday. The player is currently with the Ghana squad in Boston, USA.

FIFA stated that they are not involved in the immigration processes of host countries, including visa adjudications. The Canadian government has not yet responded to requests for comment on the matter.

Partey will be eligible to play in Ghana's subsequent Group L matches against England in Boston and Croatia in Philadelphia. The 32-year-old former Arsenal player currently plays for Villarreal.

The midfielder faces allegations of rape and sexual assault in the United Kingdom, which he has denied. This legal situation may be a factor in the visa refusal.

headline_marked: [[Bangladesh budget]] faces doubts on inflation, jobs, bank reforms, revenue
headline: Bangladesh budget faces doubts on inflation, jobs, bank reforms, revenue
summary: Ministers defend the ambitious Tk 9.38 trillion budget, but critics question its realism amid persistent inflation, weak investment, and banking sector concerns.
details: Bangladesh's new government has unveiled an expansive budget aiming for a trillion-dollar economy, lower inflation, and increased prosperity. However, questions linger about the feasibility of these ambitious targets, particularly concerning inflation, job creation, banking reforms, and revenue collection.

Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury defended the Tk 9.38 trillion budget, emphasizing its inclusive nature and a departure from the 'patronage economy' of the past. The government aims to reduce inflation to 7.5 percent, boost economic growth to 6.5 percent, and collect a record Tk 6.95 trillion in revenue.

Despite the government's assurances, economists and business leaders have raised concerns about the budget's realistic assumptions. The proposed budget is 19 percent larger than the previous year's, introduced at a time of stubborn inflation, subdued private investment, and ongoing pressure on foreign exchange reserves.

Business groups have welcomed investment incentives, but analysts doubt their sufficiency to address deeper economic problems. The National Board of Revenue's capacity to meet the ambitious revenue target has also been questioned, with think tanks like the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) warning that the projections are built on fragile ground.

Job creation remains a significant concern, with ministers offering few specifics on how many jobs will be created, in which sectors, or over what timeframe. While the government points to tax incentives and skills development, the link between investment and employment lacks measurable targets.

Questions about the source of investment are also prominent. Despite tax breaks and incentives, businesses face high borrowing costs and liquidity constraints. The budget's reliance on investment to drive growth is further complicated by concerns over the banking sector's ability to provide necessary financing.

The budget also faces scrutiny over energy security. With global energy markets unsettled, the plan to secure reliable electricity and gas supplies to meet growth targets remains a point of concern, especially given ongoing conflicts in West Asia.
